lectures.title: System Insights: Files in the Folder `/proc`

cues.en: In this lecture.
We want to have a closer look at the folder slash proc.
This folder allows us to easily inspect our system, and for that we can look into the files into the
slash proc folder.
Why would we want to inspect our system?
Well, let's say we are not the authors of that system.
In a sense.
We have not built that computer ourselves.
But let's say, for example, we are just renting a machine and the vendor has promised us a certain
amount of CPU power and a certain amount of memory.
Then inspecting the files in slash proc can give us at least an estimate whether this information can
be can be trusted or not.
So if we want to inspect our system, we can look into the files, into the folder.
So for example, we could look into the slash proc cpuinfo file.
And this contains information about the system CPUs and it shows things like vendor model and speed
and additional features.
Let's have a look at that, how that looks here.
So here I'm logged in into a virtual machine and I can just output the file proc cpuinfo to list information
about my processors.
This file is quite long because we have multiple CPUs available to our system, so here we can see the
information about our first core.
Please note depending on your processor, your processor might support a feature called Hyperthreading,
which means that one physical core might appear as two logical cores to our operating system in order
to run even more applications at the same time.
And in that case, it might be listed two times here because this will print how our operating system
sees those cores.
So just as an example, maybe a few years ago we might have had a dual core with hyper threading and
that would look like a quad core to our system so that our system can feed enough tasks to our processor
to fully utilize it.
So but that depends on your processor, whether it supports that feature or not.
But this is our first logical processor or core here that we have in our system.
We can see here it's an Intel CPU.
We can see this is the generation that I'm using here.
It's already an older CPU by now.
We can also see this is the speed that this processor can run at.
We can see the cache and we can also see that this processor supports certain CPU features or flags
called here.
What's up with those flags?
What do they mean?
Well, we can imagine it like this, that the processor supports the general tasks or the general commands
that our applications expect, but it can also support additional commands that maybe not all processors
support.
This is referring to the low level instruction code that our processor can execute.
And if it has certain flags or certain features here, for example, those here, but also the others,
they have a different idea here that they extend the the instruction set that our processor can understand.
This could, for example, be that instead of multiplying multiple numbers together with a single with
a single instruction each, we could also have a combined command, for example, that can multiply
several matrices together in just one single instruction that our that that we need to send to our processor.
And then it can work on maybe like eight multiplications at the same time.
And you can imagine that this is way faster than if we would have to multiply eight numbers individually
with separate instructions.
It's a little bit like instead of just doing one thing after the other, we can be like, Hey, do those
eight multiplications at the same time as fast as you can and then let's continue our program.
And this is extremely important.
Those CPU features.
For example, if you want to work with a lot of data that could be video transcoding training neural
network, though you should rather do that on a graphical on a GPU.
But if your application can use those features, then it usually gives a huge boost to the performance.
Now if we just scroll down, we can also see we have the next processor here, that's the next logical
core here.
It's from the same CPU here and yeah, it just repeats it.
Then we have the next processor that's now processor three.
And then if we scroll down, then we see this is our fourth core and if we keep scrolling down then
that's it with our CPU info file.
But if we look into the documentation here of this CPU.
This CPU should have 20 threads or 20 logical cores or 12 physical cores, but it should count until
19 here and not just stop at three.
Why does it stop at three?
Well, this is a virtual machine and when I created that virtual machine, I told my virtual machine
software that I only want this virtual machine to be able to use four CPUs.
So we are limited here and we are not able to use the full power.
So this is something, for example, you could check whether you get the number of threads here and
what kind of hardware your virtual machine that has been provided to you is running on.
It may also be, by the way, that if the host if one computer runs multiple virtual machines at the
same time, that it shows up here, but that you can't use the full power of one core because maybe
on the same computer there are multiple virtual machines running at the same time and the host doesn't
give the full performance to your computer, but at least you get a quick or a good overview what kind
of hardware your system is running on.
The next thing I would like to mention would be proc meminfo, which is pretty much similar to the CPU
info.
It just gives you information about the memory that your that your system is using.
So if we output that one cut proc meminfo then you can see here right now if I scroll up here, we got
eight gigabytes of memory available, 6.8GB about our free.
I say about here because technically if we want to turn this into megabytes, we would have to divide
it by 1024.
That's the factor here.
But we can see here there's enough memory available.
It also gives us additional things here.
For example, this is the memory that's available in a sense that some of the memory that we are using
could be purged or we would not necessarily need that one.
So we do have enough memory here available, but this could we could also use this one if we get a virtual
machine or something like this to confirm, do we actually have access to the promised memory that our
vendor promised to us?
The next file would be proc version that contains version information about the kernel.
Our compiler, for example here, the C plus plus compiler and our operating system.
So we can also just output that one proc version.
So I will output this one and we can see here, this is my current kernel and I'm running this is my
compiler that has been used here to compile that kernel.
So this gives us a rough idea what kind of Linux we are running on here.
Another file is proc uptime.
This displays the time that the system has been up and the amount of time it has been idle.
So if we just exit or output that file proc uptime, then we can see here it has been running for this
many seconds and it has been idle for this many seconds.
Why is it idling more than it has been running here?
This is because we got four CPU cores here right now in my system.
And if one of those is idling, then it already counts this one up.
So you can see here a few seconds later here, just about 18 seconds have passed.
And here you can see that we have a significantly higher number because, again, we have four cores
and they can all idle at the same time.
So this gives us an overview or we can use this as an overview about our uptime and how our system is
running.
The next command would be or file would be proc load avg load average.
And this shows us the load average for the past one, five and 15 minutes, followed by the number of
currently running processes and then the number of threads that are on our system in total.
And then the last process ID that we have started.
So if I just cut that one proc load avg, then we can see here the load average is that it's using 0.03
cores here in the last minute, 0.02 cores in the last five minutes and in the last 15 minutes, zero
cores of CPU power.
So this can be above one.
If we are using more than one core, we have one process running and 442 threads that are that also
might be in the background.
And this is the last process that has been started here on our system.
So you can see how all of those files here in the proc folder give you information about the hardware
that your system is running on.
Please note there are way more files in that folder, but the list that we have looked at that are the
most common ones.
But I just want you to be aware that in the proc folder this allows you to inspect your hardware and
this information can be found in this folder.
So this would be our proc folder.
They are not real files here.
They are.
I mean, they are.
Real faults, but in a sense that we can use them as if they were real files, that we can read them,
but they are generated on the fly with always up to date information.
And this folder you can use to inspect your system's resources and what's available there.
